communications.subject: RE: Freedom of Information Act Request #FOIA-2027-00003
communications.communication:
Thank you for your letter. 

I request a waiver of all fees. If the waiver is denied, I agree to pay fees up to $100, and I ask that you contact me before incurring anything higher. I am not a commercial requester. I ask to be placed in the "all other requesters" fee category, which includes two hours of search time and 100 pages (or the electronic equivalent) at no charge. Because I am asking for an electronic export of existing records, I expect duplication costs to be minimal.

Fee waiver request

Disclosure is in the public interest because it is likely to contribute significantly to public understanding of the operations or activities of the government, and it is not primarily in my commercial interest. 5 U.S.C. § 552(a)(4)(A)(iii).

1. The records concern identifiable operations of the government. The records document one specific FMCS program. Under 29 U.S.C. § 173 and Section 8(d) of the National Labor Relations Act, FMCS offers mediation to parties bargaining a first contract. Since about 2003, it has opened those cases partly from certifications the NLRB sends it. The records show:
- which newly certified units FMCS opened cases for;
- how long the cases lasted;
- how each case was closed: agreement reached, parties failed to respond, facility closed, or otherwise.

These are FMCS's own records of how it carries out a statutory duty.

2. The records are meaningfully informative and not already public. FMCS publishes F-7 notice data, but it does not publish the outcomes of its initial-contract cases. My earlier request, FOIA-2022-00042, produced only the cases closed as "Agreement Reached". The public therefore sees FMCS's successes but not its full caseload.

The only published study using comparable FMCS case records covers 1999–2004 (Ferguson, Industrial and Labor Relations Review, 2008), and those records are not public. Using the public F-7 and NLRB data alone, I have found that only about a third of units newly certified since 1999 later show a renewed contract. Public data cannot show whether the rest never reached a first contract, reached one and lost it, or never had an FMCS case at all. The requested records answer that question directly.

Policy researchers have pointed to this gap. A 2026 Economic Policy Institute report observes that the role of employer-side law firms in "frustrating workers' attempts to reach a first contract has largely gone unexamined" (Poydock, Wiggin and McNicholas 2026). FMCS's case records are the only systematic federal record of what happens in first-contract bargaining.

3. Disclosure will reach a reasonably broad audience, and I have the ability and expertise to deliver it. Since 2021, I have maintained labordata (https://labordata.bunkum.us/), a free public warehouse of 15 federal labor datasets. It includes NLRB case and election records, FMCS F-7 notices and work-stoppage data, voluntary recognitions, OSHA and Wage and Hour enforcement records, and Department of Labor union and employer disclosure filings. It needs no login, and offers a web interface, an API, CSV export and direct database queries.

It is heavily used. Over the most recent three months, labordata answered roughly 48,000 data queries, after excluding automated crawlers, from more than 300 distinct client applications. It also receives a few thousand browser visits a month. Its users include:
- university researchers;
- a labor-watchdog nonprofit that queries it daily;
- union researchers
- labor-relations consultants;

In a single recent week, users connected from the networks of at least seven universities, including UCLA, NYU and Penn State.

Researchers and policy organizations rely on it:
- Pezold, Jäger and Nüss, "Labor Market Tightness and Union Activity" (NBER Working Paper 31988, 2023), measures strikes using the FMCS work-stoppage data I collected and published.
- The Economic Policy Institute's 2026 report on employer spending on union avoidance, which examines the firms involved in "the stalling of first contract negotiations", uses NLRB data from labordata and cites it as a source (Poydock, Wiggin and McNicholas 2026).

I will release these records on labordata, free of charge and with documentation, joined to NLRB election records so that each case can be traced to the certification that started it. I will also publish an analysis of first-contract outcomes by year, industry and region.

Linking FMCS case records to NLRB certifications takes specialized knowledge of both agencies' data. I have already built that linkage for the F-7 notices, so the public will get usable information rather than a raw extract.

4. The contribution to public understanding will be significant. No public source today says how often FMCS's first-contract cases end in agreement, or how many newly certified units FMCS reaches at all. Timely first contracts are a matter of active national policy debate. The PRO Act, for example, would establish "a bargaining process for reaching a first contract in a timely manner", with FMCS mediation and arbitration (Poydock, Wiggin and McNicholas 2026). Evaluating such proposals requires knowing how FMCS's existing first-contract program performs. These records would provide the first public measure of that in two decades.

5. The request is not primarily in my commercial interest. I have no commercial interest in these records. labordata is noncommercial, and everything it publishes is free.

If FMCS grants only part of the waiver, I ask for a waiver of whatever portion of the fees qualifies. If the waiver is denied, I agree to pay fees up to $100, and I ask that you contact me before incurring anything higher.

Sincerely,
Forest Gregg

communications.subject: North Dakota Open Records Law Request: Deaths-in-custody
communications.communication:
To Whom It May Concern:

Pursuant to the North Dakota Open Records Law, I hereby request the following records:

The database or records of all law enforcement agencies deaths-in-custody up to the date this request is ultimately fulfilled, including all deaths-in-custody reported pursuant to federal legislation (34 U.S.C. § 60105), as well as all data dictionaries, database scheme documentation or other documentation on the collection and organization of the data. 

I request these records in their native digital formats and not in formats that degrade the accessibility of the records, such as tabular data converted to PDF or Word files. If converting the native digital format to another high-fidelity format, such as CSV or Excel, please take care not to introduce formatting inconsistencies or errors, which can occur in the conversion process (for example, encoding errors or the inclusion of internal unescaped quotation marks in CSV files). Should the records above represent certain values as numeric codes or abbreviations that are not self-explanatory, we additionally request all records necessary to interpret those codes and abbreviations.

The requested documents will be made available to the general public, and this request is not being made for commercial purposes.

In the event that there are fees, I would be grateful if you would inform me of the total charges in advance of fulfilling my request. I would prefer the request filled electronically, by e-mail attachment if available or CD-ROM if not.

Thank you in advance for your anticipated cooperation in this matter. I look forward to receiving your response to this request within 10 business days.

Sincerely,

Dillon Bergin
